[[File:Arizona_Removal_Operations_Coordination_Center.jpg|thumb|A view of the Arizona Removal Operations Coordination Center at Phoenix-Mesa Gateway Airport in Mesa, AZ]]
The '''Arizona Removal Operations Coordination Center''' ('''AROCC''') is an [[immigration detention]] site and flight coordination office operated by United States [[United States Immigration and Customs Enforcement|Immigration and Customs Enforcement]] (ICE) at the [[Mesa Gateway Airport|Phoenix-Mesa Gateway Airport]]. It is the headquarters of ICE Air Operations, which operates charter flights to deport immigrants from the United States. 

The site is owned by the Mesa-Gateway Airport Authority and leased to Strategic Government Properties.<ref>{{Cite web |last=MacDonald-Evoy |first=Jerod |date=2026-04-27 |title=Mesa can't enforce its own fire codes at an ICE facility where detainees can't even sit down |url=https://azmirror.com/2026/04/27/mesa-cant-enforce-its-own-fire-codes-at-an-ice-facility-where-detainees-cant-even-sit-down/ |access-date=2026-05-22 |website=Arizona Mirror |language=en-US}}</ref> Many of the flights themselves are coordinated by CSI Aviation, which subcontracted with [[Avelo Airlines]], [[GlobalX]], and Omni Air, among other private carriers.<ref>{{Cite web |date=2026-01-08 |title=Avelo Airlines withdraws from ICE deportation operations, closes Mesa Gateway base |url=https://azmirror.com/briefs/avelo-airlines-withdraws-from-ice-deportation-operations-closes-mesa-gateway-base/ |access-date=2026-05-22 |website=Arizona Mirror |language=en-US}}</ref> Avelo withdrew from serving AROCC in January 2026.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Avelo Airlines withdraws from ICE deportation operations, closes Mesa Gateway base |url=https://azmirror.com/briefs/avelo-airlines-withdraws-from-ice-deportation-operations-closes-mesa-gateway-base/ |access-date=2026-05-22 |website=Arizona Mirror |language=en-US}}</ref> 

== Capacity and overcrowding ==
The Center opened in 2010 with a planned capacity of 157 detainees and 79 ICE employees.<ref>{{Cite web |last=MacDonald-Evoy |first=Jerod |date=2025-08-29 |title=The ICE Facility in Phoenix you probably didn’t know existed |url=https://azmirror.com/2025/08/29/the-ice-facility-in-phoenix-you-probably-didnt-know-existed/ |access-date=2026-05-22 |website=Arizona Mirror |language=en-US}}</ref> A 2022 audit described the facility as a single-floor building with "10 multiple occupancy hold rooms with a total design capacity of 157."<ref name=":0">{{Cite conference |last=Ames |first=Marlean |date=2022-08-03 |title=PREA Audit: Arizona Removal Operations Coordination Center |url=https://www.ice.gov/doclib/foia/prea_audit/arizonaRemovalOpsCoordinationCntr_Aug2-3_2022.pdf |publisher=Department of Homeland Security |access-date=2026-05-22}}</ref> The facility also lacks beds, showers, educational or library facilities,  a medical clinic, designated food service areas, and recreation facilities.<ref name=":0" /> 

Between early 2025 and early 2026, the average population at AROCC rose from 21 prisoners per day to 276 per day.<ref name=":1">{{Cite web |last=MacDonald-Evoy |first=Jerod |date=2026-04-30 |title=Mesa airport warns ICE facility's landlord that overcrowding may violate its lease |url=https://azmirror.com/2026/04/30/mesa-airport-warns-ice-facilitys-landlord-that-overcrowding-may-violate-its-lease/ |access-date=2026-05-22 |website=Arizona Mirror |language=en-US}}</ref>

In January 2026, the Mesa Fire and Medical Department, which had responded to a medical emergency issued a list of code violations for AROCC. The facility had housed 238 people at the time, well above the building's fire capacity of 203 individuals. However, the population soon rose, reaching 646, 526, and 777 individuals on later days in 2026.<ref>{{Cite web |last=MacDonald-Evoy |first=Jerod |date=2026-04-30 |title=Mesa airport warns ICE facility's landlord that overcrowding may violate its lease |url=https://azmirror.com/2026/04/30/mesa-airport-warns-ice-facilitys-landlord-that-overcrowding-may-violate-its-lease/ |access-date=2026-05-22 |website=Arizona Mirror |language=en-US}}</ref> Three members of Congress reported "shocking" overcrowding in April, after visiting on a day when there were around 250 detainees.<ref name=":1" /><ref>{{cite news |title=Mesa ICE Holding Site Called 'Sickening' By Arizona Democrats |url=https://hoodline.com/2026/02/mesa-s-hidden-ice-hub-branded-sickening-after-surprise-lawmaker-tour/ |access-date=14 April 2026 |work=[[Hoodline]] |date=21 February 2026 |language=en}}</ref>

Like other ICE hold facilities, AROCC is classified as a "12-hour facility," theoretically limiting detainee stays to a maximum of twelve hours. However, this cap has repeatedly been exceeded. In June 2025, 77 detainees being prepared for an Omni Air flight stayed at AROCC for four days. The flight later deported migrants to Bangladesh and Pakistan.<ref>{{Cite news |last=Dingman |first=Sam |date=2025-09-02 |title=New report reveals troubling details about an ICE facility at Phoenix-Mesa Gateway Airport |url=https://www.kjzz.org/text/the-show/2025-09-02/new-report-reveals-troubling-details-about-an-ice-facility-at-phoenix-mesa-gateway-airport |access-date=2026-05-22 |work=KJZZ}}</ref>

== Flight operations ==
[[File:ICE agent stands by aircraft for removal flight.jpg|thumb|Uniformed agent of Immigration and Customs Enforcement stands by a plane as part of removal operations]]
In 2025, 778 ICE flights departed from the facility. There were 338 flights in the first quarter of 2026.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Walker |first=Austin |date=2026-05-06 |title=Concerns grow over potential overcrowding at Mesa Gateway ICE facility |url=https://www.azfamily.com/2026/05/06/concerns-grow-over-potential-overcrowding-mesa-gateway-ice-facility/ |access-date=2026-05-22 |website=Arizona Family |language=en}}</ref>
